laws.title: Fundamental Law of Hungary
laws.subtitle: Alaptörvény — Hungary's Constitution (2011)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2011 Fundamental Law replaced the communist-era 1949 constitution (as amended in 1989). Enacted by Viktor Orbán's Fidesz supermajority, it has been amended 12+ times. It entrenches Christian heritage, defines marriage as between a man and a woman, restricts the Constitutional Court's jurisdiction over budget laws, and allows indefinite detention of asylum seekers. The Venice Commission of the Council of Europe has repeatedly criticized the constitution for concentrating power. Hungary moved from a parliamentary republic to a 'hybrid regime' in international assessments under Fidesz rule.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for constitutional violations; Constitutional Court has limited jurisdiction post-2011 reforms.
exceptions: Constitutional Court retains jurisdiction over fundamental rights outside budget matters
Emergency (special legal order) provisions allow government decree rule

quiz.q: What replaced Hungary's communist-era constitution in 2011?
quiz.explanation: Hungary's 2011 Fundamental Law (Alaptörvény) replaced the Soviet-era 1949 constitution that had been amended in 1989. Enacted by Viktor Orbán's Fidesz supermajority, it significantly concentrated political power and has been repeatedly criticized by the Venice Commission.

laws.title: Rule of Law Crisis and EU Conflicts
laws.subtitle: EU Article 7 Procedure and Conditionality Mechanism
laws.fullDescription: The European Commission triggered Article 7(1) TEU proceedings against Hungary in 2018 over rule of law concerns—courts, media, universities, civil society, migration, corruption. The EU's new conditionality mechanism (2022) froze approximately €22 billion in EU cohesion funds to Hungary over governance concerns. Hungary has been declared a 'hybrid regime' or 'electoral autocracy' by Freedom House and V-Dem. The Sargentini Report detailed systemic threats to EU values. Hungary and Poland have often formed a blocking minority against EU sanctions. In 2024, some funds were partially released after Hungary undertook judicial reforms.
laws.penalty: No domestic criminal penalties; EU fund conditionality creates financial incentives for reform.
exceptions: Hungary disputes all EU rule of law assessments as political interference
National sovereignty over constitutional arrangements is argued by Hungarian government

quiz.q: Approximately how much EU funding was frozen by the conditionality mechanism over Hungary's rule of law concerns?
quiz.explanation: The EU's Rule of Law Conditionality Mechanism froze approximately €22 billion in EU cohesion and recovery funds to Hungary in 2022 over governance and rule of law concerns, the largest such freeze applied to any EU member state.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Child Protection Law
laws.subtitle: 2021 Anti-LGBTQ+ Law (Child Protection Amendment)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2021 law banned content 'promoting' homosexuality or gender change to under-18s—covering education, advertising, TV, and internet. The law was condemned by 17 EU member states, the European Parliament, and the EU Commission as discriminatory and incompatible with EU law. The Commission launched infringement proceedings. Hungary framed it as parental rights and child protection. In a 2022 referendum, Orbán asked voters if they supported the law—turnout was high enough to be valid but results were disputed. LGBTQ+ Hungarians face significant social hostility and legal discrimination.
laws.penalty: Media outlets violating content rules: fines from the media authority. Educational institutions: license review.
exceptions: Medical and scientific information (differently framed) may be permitted
Information about historical events not subject to same restrictions

quiz.q: How did the EU Commission respond to Hungary's 2021 anti-LGBTQ+ law?
options: Launched infringement proceedings and condemned it as incompatible with EU law
Accepted it under national sovereignty provisions
Referred it to the European Court of Human Rights
quiz.explanation: The European Commission launched infringement proceedings against Hungary's 2021 anti-LGBTQ+ law, concluding it was incompatible with EU law and fundamental rights. Seventeen EU member states signed a joint statement condemning the law as discriminatory.

laws.title: Media Law and Press Freedom
laws.subtitle: Media Services and Mass Communications Act (2010)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2010 media law created the National Media and Infocommunications Authority (NMHH) and the Media Council—both filled with Fidesz loyalists. The law requires 'balanced' coverage and allows fines for vague content violations. Within a decade, approximately 80% of Hungarian media came under pro-Fidesz ownership through politically connected businesspeople. State advertising is channeled exclusively to pro-government outlets. Independent outlets (444.hu, Telex, Márton Gulyás) operate under economic pressure. RSF World Press Freedom Index ranks Hungary 72nd (2023), the lowest in the EU. Reporters Without Borders has documented systematic media capture.
laws.penalty: Media Council fines up to 200 million HUF for content violations. License revocation for repeat offenders.
exceptions: Online media has somewhat lighter regulation than broadcast
International media freely accessible (but constrained by state ad boycott)

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Hungarian media came under pro-Fidesz ownership by 2020?
quiz.explanation: By approximately 2020, roughly 80% of Hungarian media had come under pro-Fidesz ownership—through politically connected businesspeople donating outlets to a central foundation (KESMA), channeling state advertising, and creating economic pressure on independent media—making Hungary an outlier in EU press freedom.

laws.title: Judicial Independence Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Judiciary Reform Laws (2011-2019)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's post-2010 judicial reforms lowered the mandatory retirement age for judges from 70 to 62, effectively forcing out hundreds of experienced judges and allowing politically loyal replacements. The Constitutional Court's jurisdiction was curtailed over budget laws. The National Judicial Office (OBH) was created with a president appointed by parliament (and thus by Fidesz majority)—allowing case allocation manipulation. The Venice Commission criticized these reforms as undermining judicial independence. EU infringement proceedings challenged the retirement age change. The Kúria (Supreme Court) president was replaced. International assessments rate Hungarian judicial independence as severely compromised.
laws.penalty: No direct criminal penalties; judicial reforms changed appointment and career structures.
exceptions: Individual judges retain formal independence in deciding cases
Constitutional Court retains some independence in non-fiscal matters

quiz.q: What judicial reform did Hungary make in 2011 that forced out hundreds of experienced judges?
options: Lowered mandatory retirement age from 70 to 62
Required all judges to reapply for positions
Required parliamentary approval for all judicial appointments
quiz.explanation: Hungary lowered the mandatory judicial retirement age from 70 to 62 in 2011, forcing approximately 274 experienced judges (many with democratic reform credentials) into early retirement, allowing Fidesz-aligned majorities to appoint more politically sympathetic replacements. The EU challenged this as discriminatory.

laws.title: Migration and Asylum Law
laws.subtitle: Border Closures and Transit Zone System
laws.fullDescription: Hungary built a fence on its Serbian and Croatian borders in 2015 during the refugee crisis and declared a 'migration emergency' that remains in force. Transit zones on the border were used to detain asylum seekers indefinitely. The European Court of Human Rights ruled this violated human rights (2021). Hungary's Stop Soros law (2018) criminalized helping asylum seekers—organizations assisting migrants could face criminal prosecution. The EU Commission launched infringement proceedings. Hungary refuses EU asylum relocation quotas. Orbán's anti-immigration rhetoric is central to Fidesz political identity.
laws.penalty: Stop Soros: providing assistance to asylum seekers enabling legal residence: up to 1 year imprisonment.
exceptions: Hungarians providing purely humanitarian aid (food, water) not covered by 'Stop Soros'
Diplomatic and consular staff processing legal migration unaffected

quiz.q: What did Hungary's 'Stop Soros' law of 2018 criminalize?
options: Providing assistance to asylum seekers enabling legal residence
Participating in civil society organizations funded by foreign donors
quiz.explanation: Hungary's 'Stop Soros' law criminalized providing assistance to asylum seekers that could help them file asylum claims or obtain legal residence, with up to 1 year imprisonment. Named after George Soros (a Hungarian-born philanthropist who funds civil society), the law targeted NGOs helping refugees and asylum seekers.

laws.title: Special Economic Taxes
laws.subtitle: Sectoral Taxes (Banks, Telecoms, Retail)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary introduced special 'windfall' and crisis taxes on banks, telecommunications, retail, energy, and pharmaceutical companies—often retroactively applied. The 2022 windfall tax on banks was 8x the regular tax rate. Companies frequently complain about unpredictable tax environment affecting investment. The Robin Hood Tax on banks was introduced in 2010. The National Bank of Hungary (MNB) under György Matolcsy accumulated unusual assets. Hungary also imposes a financial transaction levy and insurance tax. EU state aid rules have been invoked against some measures. The tax system is seen as designed to benefit politically connected businesses over foreign multinationals.
laws.penalty: Tax non-compliance: standard penalties plus 50% surcharge. Sectoral tax evasion: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Small businesses below 500 million HUF revenue exempt from sectoral taxes
Domestic SMEs often receive more favorable treatment than multinationals

quiz.q: What unusual sectoral taxes did Hungary introduce that have been criticized for unpredictability?
options: Special windfall taxes on banks, telecoms, retail, and energy
Import tariff surcharges on EU goods
quiz.explanation: Hungary introduced special sectoral taxes on banks, telecommunications companies, retailers, and energy firms—often retroactively and at very high rates. The 2022 bank windfall tax was 8 times the regular tax rate. These measures have been widely criticized for creating an unpredictable investment environment.

laws.title: Family Policy and Pro-Natalist Programs
laws.subtitle: Family Protection Action Plan
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has aggressive pro-natalist policies under Orbán, framed as promoting 'Hungarian families' rather than immigration. The CSOK (Home Purchase Subsidy Program) offers up to 10 million HUF grant for third child. Women with four or more children are exempt from income tax for life. Low-interest loans (up to 10 million HUF) are given to young married couples, forgiven on third child. Childcare is subsidized. Hungary spends approximately 5% of GDP on family policies—one of the highest globally. Despite massive spending, fertility has risen only modestly (from 1.23 in 2011 to about 1.5 in 2022) and fell again in 2023.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; benefits are positive incentives rather than punishments for non-compliance.
exceptions: Same-sex couples excluded from CSOK and most family benefits
Foreign nationals have more limited access to benefits

quiz.q: What income tax benefit do Hungarian women with four or more children receive?
options: Permanent income tax exemption for life
One-time tax rebate of 2 million HUF
quiz.explanation: Under Hungary's pro-natalist family policy, women who give birth to four or more children are permanently exempt from personal income tax for the rest of their lives—one of the most generous pro-natalist tax measures anywhere in the world.

laws.title: Electoral Law and Gerrymandering
laws.subtitle: Act on Electoral Procedure (2011)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2011 electoral reform reduced parliament from 386 to 199 seats, redrew constituency boundaries (widely seen as gerrymandering favoring Fidesz), and eliminated the two-round system. In 2022, Fidesz won 54% of votes but 68% of seats due to the electoral system design. Constituency boundaries strongly favor rural areas where Fidesz dominates over urban areas. Party list registration requirements make it difficult for new parties to compete. Campaign finance rules allow state resources to be used for government communications that function as election advertising. OSCE monitoring missions have criticized Hungary's elections.
laws.penalty: Electoral fraud: criminal prosecution. Campaign finance violations: fines.
exceptions: Small parties with fewer signatures may participate in regional lists
Diaspora Hungarians voting in party lists only

quiz.q: How did Hungary's 2022 election result demonstrate the impact of the 2011 electoral reform?
options: Fidesz won 54% of votes but 68% of seats due to gerrymandering
Fidesz lost seats despite winning the popular vote
The opposition won more seats despite fewer votes
quiz.explanation: In Hungary's 2022 election, Fidesz received approximately 54% of the popular vote but translated this into 68% of parliamentary seats, demonstrating how the 2011 electoral reform—including redrawn constituency boundaries and reduced parliament size—was structured to benefit the ruling party.

laws.title: University Autonomy and CEU
laws.subtitle: National Higher Education Act (2017 Amendment)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2017 amendment to the Higher Education Act targeted Central European University (CEU), founded by George Soros in Budapest. The law required universities with 'foreign' in their name to also operate in their home country and obtain a bilateral government agreement. CEU had to relocate its accredited programs to Vienna (2019) while maintaining a presence in Budapest. The European Court of Justice ruled the law violated EU law (2020). More broadly, university autonomy has been curtailed—several universities were placed under foundations controlled by Fidesz-aligned trustees, removing state universities from direct government control but also from traditional academic governance.
laws.penalty: Universities not complying with registration requirements: license revocation.
exceptions: State universities retain some operational autonomy within trustee-controlled foundations
Religious universities operate under separate legal frameworks

quiz.q: Which university was effectively forced out of Budapest by Hungary's 2017 higher education law amendment?
quiz.explanation: Central European University (CEU), founded by Hungarian-American philanthropist George Soros, was the primary target of Hungary's 2017 higher education law amendment. CEU was forced to relocate its accredited programs to Vienna in 2019, though it maintained a presence in Budapest. The ECJ later ruled the law violated EU standards.

laws.title: State Capitalism and National Champions
laws.subtitle: Strategic Sectors Law and State Enterprise Policy
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has pursued a 'national capitalism' model since 2010—expanding state ownership in strategic sectors (energy, banking, media, retail) while favoring politically connected domestic oligarchs. OTP Bank remains majority privately owned but with significant state influence. MOL (oil and gas) is partly state-owned. The MVM group was expanded to control much of Hungary's energy sector. Lőrinc Mészáros, a childhood friend of Orbán, became Hungary's richest person through government contracts in construction, media, and banking. International transparency organizations rate Hungary as having serious corruption and crony capitalism problems.
laws.penalty: Corruption: criminal prosecution but low conviction rates for politically connected individuals.
exceptions: State-owned enterprises have different procurement rules allowing direct contracting
EU-funded projects subject to EU audit and anti-fraud rules (OLAF investigations)

quiz.q: Who became Hungary's richest person through government contracts after being Viktor Orbán's childhood friend?
quiz.explanation: Lőrinc Mészáros, a former gas fitter and childhood friend of Prime Minister Orbán, became Hungary's richest person after 2010, accumulating a vast fortune through government contracts in construction, media, banking, and hospitality. His rapid enrichment is widely cited as evidence of crony capitalism in Hungary.

laws.title: State of Emergency Powers
laws.subtitle: Fundamental Law Special Legal Orders Provisions
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's Fundamental Law contains extensive emergency power provisions (Special Legal Order). During COVID-19, the National Assembly granted the government unlimited power to rule by decree (March 2020)—an unprecedented move widely criticized as exploiting the pandemic. The Act on Protection against Coronavirus gave Orbán powers with no sunset clause for the first version. The EU Parliament condemned this. Hungary also declared a special legal order in response to the Russia-Ukraine war (2022) and migration (ongoing since 2015). Critics argue these powers have become a permanent governance tool to bypass parliament.
laws.penalty: Violation of emergency decrees: criminal prosecution with accelerated procedures during emergency.
exceptions: Parliament retains formal power to revoke emergency authorization (though Fidesz holds supermajority)
Constitutional Court retains jurisdiction (though limited by 2011 reforms)

quiz.q: What unprecedented action did Hungary's parliament take during the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020?
options: Granted the government unlimited power to rule by decree with no sunset clause
Suspended all elections for one year
Transferred all powers to the president
quiz.explanation: In March 2020, Hungary's National Assembly—where Fidesz holds a supermajority—granted the government unlimited power to rule by decree during the COVID-19 pandemic, initially with no sunset clause. The EU Parliament condemned this as an exploitation of the pandemic to expand executive power.

laws.title: Religious Freedom and State Church Relationships
laws.subtitle: Church Act (2011)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2011 Church Act deregistered over 300 previously recognized religious groups, leaving only 14 'recognized churches' eligible for state funding and tax benefits. Groups deregistered included many Protestant, Buddhist, and new religious movements. The Venice Commission condemned this as violating religious freedom. Re-registration required two-thirds parliamentary vote—an inherently political process. The dominant historical churches (Catholic, Calvinist, Lutheran) retained privileged status. The Constitutional Court partially struck down the law; amended versions continued the policy. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled against Hungary on religious freedom grounds.
laws.penalty: Organizations operating as churches without recognized status cannot receive state benefits; no criminal prohibition on worship.
exceptions: Unrecognized religious groups may operate as civil associations
Individual religious practice is not restricted—only state recognition and funding

quiz.q: How many religious groups did Hungary's 2011 Church Act deregister?
quiz.explanation: Hungary's 2011 Church Act removed state recognition from over 300 previously recognized religious groups, leaving only 14 'recognized churches' eligible for state funding and tax benefits. The Venice Commission condemned this as a serious violation of religious freedom, requiring a two-thirds parliamentary vote for re-recognition.

laws.title: Anti-Corruption Law (in Theory)
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code — Corruption Provisions
laws.fullDescription: Hungary formally criminalizes corruption—bribery, embezzlement of public funds, trading in influence. However, Hungary scores poorly on anti-corruption indices: Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index ranked Hungary 77th globally in 2022, the lowest in the EU. OLAF (EU Anti-Fraud Office) has documented extensive misuse of EU funds involving politically connected entities. The anti-corruption prosecutor's office has been criticized for inaction on politically sensitive cases. The Integrity Authority (established 2022 under EU pressure) has conducted some oversight. Major corruption scandals involving EU fund diversion have been documented by Hungarian investigative outlet Direkt36.
laws.penalty: Active bribery of public official: up to 5 years imprisonment. Embezzlement of public funds: up to 8 years.
exceptions: Whistleblower protections under the Whistleblower Protection Act (2023, enacted under EU pressure)
Anti-corruption reporting through Integrity Authority

quiz.q: Where does Hungary rank among EU member states on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index?
options: Among the top 5 least corrupt EU states
quiz.explanation: Hungary ranks last among EU member states on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index, with a 2022 ranking of 77th globally. OLAF investigations have documented extensive misuse of EU funds involving politically connected entities close to the Fidesz government.

laws.title: Energy Policy and Dependence on Russia
laws.subtitle: Energy Law and Paks II Nuclear Agreement
laws.fullDescription: Hungary is heavily dependent on Russian energy—about 85% of its gas and 65% of its oil came from Russia as of 2022. Prime Minister Orbán maintained close ties with Putin even after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Hungary secured exemptions from some EU energy sanctions on Russia. The Paks II nuclear plant expansion ($12 billion) is financed by Russian state loans and built by Rosatom—creating long-term strategic dependency. Hungary resisted EU energy solidarity measures. MVM Group controls much of Hungary's energy infrastructure. Despite EU pressure, Hungary's energy dependency on Russia has declined only slowly.
laws.penalty: Energy regulatory violations: Hungarian Energy and Public Utility Regulatory Authority (MEKH) enforcement.
exceptions: Paks II operates under separate international agreement exempting it from some EU procurement rules
Emergency gas storage requirements allow some national flexibility
laws.sourceLabel: Hungarian Energy and Public Utility Regulatory Authority

quiz.q: What major nuclear power project creates long-term Russian dependency for Hungary?
options: Paks II — financed by Russian loans and built by Rosatom
quiz.explanation: The Paks II nuclear power plant expansion is a $12 billion project financed by Russian state loans and constructed by Rosatom (Russia's state nuclear company), creating a long-term strategic energy dependency between Hungary and Russia that persists even during EU sanctions over the Ukraine war.

laws.title: National Minority Rights
laws.subtitle: Act on the Rights of National Minorities (2011)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has 13 recognized national minorities (German, Roma, Slovak, Romanian, Croatian, Serb, Slovenian, Polish, Greek, Bulgarian, Ruthene, Ukrainian, Armenian). Roma are the largest minority (approximately 700,000-800,000). Despite formal protections, Hungarian Roma face extreme poverty, school segregation, and discrimination. The Roma integration strategy has had limited success. Minority self-governments (cultural autonomy) exist for all 13 groups. Hungary's treatment of ethnic Hungarians in neighboring countries (Transylvania/Romania, Slovakia, Serbia) is a foreign policy priority—offering Hungarian citizenship to diaspora Hungarians (3 million abroad have received citizenship).
laws.penalty: Incitement against national minority: criminal prosecution, up to 3 years.
exceptions: Diaspora Hungarians receiving citizenship can vote in Hungarian elections (party list only)
Positive discrimination for minorities in education and employment is permitted

quiz.q: Approximately how many ethnic Hungarians living abroad have received Hungarian citizenship since diaspora citizenship was introduced?
quiz.explanation: Hungary granted citizenship to approximately 3 million ethnic Hungarians living in neighboring countries (primarily Romania's Transylvania, Slovakia, Serbia, and Ukraine), allowing them to vote in Hungarian elections (on party lists). Critics argue this was designed to benefit Fidesz politically.

laws.title: Constitutional Court Limitations
laws.subtitle: Fundamental Law Changes to Constitutional Court Jurisdiction
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's Constitutional Court was historically the most powerful such court in post-communist Europe. The 2010-2013 reforms dramatically curtailed its powers: it lost the ability to review budget laws on substantive grounds, the number of justices was increased from 11 to 15 (allowing Fidesz to appoint a majority), and the act-on-a-principle review was restricted. Most justices are now appointed by the Fidesz parliamentary majority. The Court still rules on individual constitutional complaints and some government actions but rarely challenges core Fidesz policies. This transformation is cited as a key element of Hungary's democratic backsliding.
laws.penalty: Government acts ruled unconstitutional must be revised; however, parliament can constitutionalize measures by amending the Fundamental Law.
exceptions: Court retains jurisdiction over individual fundamental rights complaints
Some EU law questions referred to ECJ for preliminary ruling

quiz.q: What happened to the size of Hungary's Constitutional Court in 2010-2013?
options: Increased from 11 to 15 justices, allowing Fidesz to appoint a majority
Kept at 11 but all existing justices were replaced
quiz.explanation: Hungary's Constitutional Court was expanded from 11 to 15 justices in 2010-2013, enabling the Fidesz parliamentary supermajority to appoint a ruling-party-aligned majority. Combined with restrictions on the Court's jurisdiction over budget matters, this effectively neutered judicial oversight of Fidesz's legislative agenda.

laws.title: Labor Law and Trade Union Rights
laws.subtitle: Labor Code (2012)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2012 Labor Code increased the permissible overtime to 400 hours per year (critics called it the 'slave law' when amended in 2018 to allow 400 cumulative hours with 3-year bank). Employers can require up to 400 hours of annual overtime with 3 years to pay it out. Mass protests in December 2018 erupted against this amendment. Trade union rights are formally protected but union density has fallen sharply under post-2010 policies. The Confederation of Hungarian Trade Unions (MSZOSZ) has been weakened. Strike rights are heavily restricted in public services. Minimum wage increases have been granted while weakening collective bargaining.
laws.penalty: Employer violation of labor code: labor authority fines. Illegal strike: civil liability for damages.
exceptions: Civil servants have separate employment law (somewhat stronger protections)
Public utility workers face strike restrictions under essential services definition

quiz.q: What nickname was given to Hungary's 2018 labor amendment allowing 400 hours of overtime with a 3-year payback period?
quiz.explanation: Hungary's 2018 amendment to the Labor Code allowing employers to demand 400 hours of overtime per year with up to 3 years to pay it out was nicknamed the 'slave law' by critics and opposition. It sparked the largest street protests in Hungary in decades, in December 2018.

laws.title: Environmental Law and Climate Policy
laws.subtitle: Act on Environmental Protection (1995, as amended)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's climate ambition is modest by EU standards. Hungary relies significantly on nuclear power (Paks plant, approximately 50% of electricity) and has relatively modest renewable energy targets. The green transition has been slower than Western EU states. River management is significant—the Danube and Tisza flow through Hungary. The controversial Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros Dam dispute with Czechoslovakia/Slovakia (ICJ case, 1997) remains a landmark in international environmental law. Air quality in Budapest and industrial areas faces challenges. Hungary blocked some EU climate legislation in 2022-2023 as leverage in other negotiations.
laws.penalty: Environmental law violations: EPA-equivalent (National Inspectorate for Environment and Nature) fines and prosecution.
exceptions: Agricultural activities under cross-compliance rules
Industrial installations under EU IPPC/IED permits have specific regulated emission limits

quiz.q: What famous international environmental law case involved Hungary and its Danube dam dispute with Czechoslovakia?
quiz.explanation: The Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros case (Hungary v. Slovakia, ICJ 1997) involved a dispute over a dam project on the Danube where Hungary withdrew from a treaty to build the dam for environmental reasons. The ICJ ruled both states had violated international obligations but the case established important precedents about state responsibility and environmental protection in international law.

laws.title: Surveillance and Intelligence Law
laws.subtitle: National Security Services Act (1995, as amended)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's intelligence framework was thrust into global spotlight by the Pegasus Project (2021): NSO Group's Pegasus spyware was used to surveil journalists, opposition politicians, lawyers, and civil society members in Hungary. Hungary is believed to have been one of NSO's most active clients. The Hungarian government confirmed it acquired surveillance tools but declined to confirm Pegasus specifically, citing national security. The constitutional framework for intelligence gathering lacks robust judicial oversight. The Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK) has broad powers. The EU Parliament's PEGA Committee investigated Hungary extensively.
laws.penalty: Illegal surveillance: criminal prosecution for unauthorized interception, up to 3 years.
exceptions: National security surveillance with designated government authorization
Counter-terrorism operations under TEK have expanded powers

quiz.q: What surveillance scandal involving Hungary was revealed by the 2021 Pegasus Project?
options: Hungary used NSO's Pegasus spyware to surveil journalists and opposition politicians
Hungary sold surveillance data to Russia
Government officials were themselves Pegasus targets
quiz.explanation: The 2021 Pegasus Project investigation revealed that Hungary used NSO Group's Pegasus spyware to surveil journalists, opposition politicians, lawyers, and civil society activists. Hungary was one of the most active Pegasus clients identified, prompting an EU Parliament investigation through the PEGA Committee.

laws.title: Healthcare System
laws.subtitle: Health Act (1997) and National Health Insurance Fund
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's public healthcare is funded through the National Health Insurance Fund (OEP/NEAK). The system is based on a Soviet-era model of large hospital networks, often with outdated facilities. Gratitude payments (hálapénz) — unofficial cash payments to doctors for better treatment — are deeply embedded in culture despite formal illegality. A 2021 reform attempted to eliminate these by significantly increasing physician salaries and banning hálapénz. Brain drain of Hungarian doctors and nurses to Western Europe (particularly UK, Germany) is severe. Waiting lists for specialized care are long. Private healthcare for those who can afford it has grown significantly.
laws.penalty: Accepting hálapénz (gratitude payments): criminal prosecution for corruption after 2021 reform. Healthcare fraud: up to 8 years.
exceptions: Voluntary patient gifts given after (not before) treatment in a non-transactional context may not constitute bribery
Private healthcare operates under separate licensing

quiz.q: What are 'hálapénz' in Hungary's healthcare system?
options: Unofficial cash payments to doctors for better treatment (gratitude payments)
quiz.explanation: Hálapénz (literally 'gratitude money') are informal cash payments made by patients to doctors in Hungary's public healthcare system to receive better or faster treatment. Despite being formally illegal (and targeted by a 2021 reform), the practice has been deeply embedded in Hungarian medical culture for decades.

laws.title: Innovation and Technology Policy
laws.subtitle: Startup Law and Research, Development, Innovation Act
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has invested in technology and innovation through the National Research, Development and Innovation Office (NKFIH). The Cybersecurity Act and Digital State Strategy aim to develop Hungary's tech sector. Prezi and LogMeIn are notable Hungarian tech successes. The Hungarian government has attracted investment from Samsung (battery plant), CATL (battery plant), and BMW (Debrecen factory)—controversial due to water usage concerns. The startup ecosystem in Budapest is growing. Tax incentives for R&D (double deduction) are available. The government has pushed 'digital Hungary' with e-government services, though concerns about digital rights shadow these initiatives.
laws.penalty: IP theft in technology sector: criminal prosecution under Criminal Code and specific IP legislation.
exceptions: R&D activities qualify for enhanced tax deductions
University spin-offs have access to preferential public funding
laws.sourceLabel: National Research, Development and Innovation Office

quiz.q: Which major battery manufacturers have invested in Hungary, controversially due to water usage concerns?
options: Samsung SDI and CATL (Chinese battery manufacturer)
quiz.explanation: Samsung SDI and CATL (the world's largest battery manufacturer, based in China) both established major battery manufacturing plants in Hungary, drawn by tax incentives and EU market access. The plants faced controversy over significant water usage in water-stressed regions of Hungary.

laws.title: Criminal Procedure and Rule of Law
laws.subtitle: Act on Criminal Procedure (2017)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2017 Code of Criminal Procedure replaced the 1998 code. The new code allows broader use of classified evidence, restricts defense access to case materials during investigation, and expands the use of confessions. European legal experts have criticized some provisions as not meeting fair trial standards under ECHR Article 6. The prosecution service (Legfőbb Ügyészség) is led by Péter Polt, a Fidesz loyalist appointed in 2010. The Constitution gives the Prosecutor General fixed 9-year terms and parliament can only remove by two-thirds—effectively immune to removal while Fidesz holds supermajority. This creates concerns about selective prosecution.
laws.penalty: Criminal procedures follow the 2017 Code; penalties depend on specific offense.
exceptions: Classified evidence provisions have specific judicial authorization requirements
Defense rights maintained formally under code provisions

quiz.q: Why is Hungary's Prosecutor General effectively immune to removal while Fidesz holds a parliamentary supermajority?
options: The constitution gives the Prosecutor General a fixed 9-year term removable only by a two-thirds vote
Prosecutors have lifetime tenure under Hungarian law
The EU prohibits removal of national prosecutors
President's veto protects the Prosecutor General
quiz.explanation: Hungary's constitution gives the Prosecutor General a fixed 9-year term and allows removal only by a two-thirds parliamentary majority. Since Fidesz holds a supermajority, opposition parties cannot remove the Fidesz-loyal Prosecutor General Péter Polt, giving the government effective control over prosecution decisions.

laws.title: Education System and Centralization
laws.subtitle: National Curriculum (2020) and Public Education Act
laws.fullDescription: Hungary centralized its entire public education system in 2012—all schools (even formerly municipal ones) are now under national administration (KLIK/EMMI/NOKS). The 2020 national curriculum was significantly revised with more emphasis on patriotism, Christian values, and Hungarian culture. Teachers' strikes (2022) over low wages drew massive public support. Hungarian teacher salaries are among the lowest in the OECD relative to GDP. The 'dual education' (apprenticeship) system was expanded. Segregation of Roma students remains a systemic problem documented by the EU and NGOs. History curriculum changes have minimized Holocaust and communist-era crimes.
laws.penalty: School non-compliance with national curriculum: administrative sanctions.
exceptions: Church-run schools maintain more autonomy under bilateral agreements
International schools for foreign nationals follow different curricula

quiz.q: What 2022 labor action by Hungarian educators drew massive public support over low wages?
quiz.explanation: Hungarian teachers staged strikes and work-to-rule actions in 2022, with massive public support, over chronically low wages—Hungarian teachers earn among the lowest salaries relative to GDP per capita in the OECD. The government's response was widely criticized as inadequate.

laws.title: EU Membership and Sovereignty Debates
laws.subtitle: Hungary's EU Relations and Sovereignty Protection Act 2023
laws.fullDescription: Hungary joined the EU in 2004 and the Schengen Area in 2007. Under Orbán, Hungary has had the most contentious relationship with EU institutions of any member state—blocking aid to Ukraine, vetoing EU sanctions packages, challenging EU asylum distribution, and blocking EU budgets pending Hungarian demands. The 2023 Sovereignty Protection Act created a Sovereignty Protection Office to investigate foreign funding of Hungarian civil society—widely seen as a tool against EU-funded NGOs and opposition groups. Hungary was blocked from EU Council presidency votes in some instances. EU Parliament repeatedly passed resolutions against Hungary.
laws.penalty: Sovereignty Protection Office can investigate and expose organizations—intimidation tool rather than criminal law.
exceptions: EU treaty obligations still legally binding on Hungary
EU citizens retain free movement rights in Hungary despite political tensions

quiz.q: What 2023 Hungarian law created a body to investigate foreign funding of civil society organizations?
options: Sovereignty Protection Act (creating Sovereignty Protection Office)
quiz.explanation: Hungary's 2023 Sovereignty Protection Act established a Sovereignty Protection Office with powers to investigate organizations receiving foreign funding, widely seen as targeting EU-funded NGOs, opposition groups, and civil society organizations critical of the government.

laws.title: Banking Regulation
laws.subtitle: Act on Credit Institutions and Financial Enterprises (2013)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's banking sector is regulated by the National Bank of Hungary (MNB), which has an unusually broad mandate including financial stability, financial supervision, and significant asset accumulation. Under Governor György Matolcsy (2013-), MNB launched controversial programs including purchasing art and real estate and establishing foundations managing billions of public assets. OTP Bank is Hungary's largest and only major domestically owned bank—government has informally promoted its regional expansion (into Slovenia, Montenegro, Bulgaria). The 2013 financial institution law implemented post-crisis EU banking reforms while maintaining national characteristics.
laws.penalty: Banking regulatory violations: MNB enforcement, fines up to 2 billion HUF for systemic institutions.
exceptions: Microfinance institutions have simplified regulatory requirements
Agricultural credit cooperatives under separate legal framework

quiz.q: What unusual activities has Hungary's National Bank (MNB) engaged in under Governor György Matolcsy?
options: Purchasing art and real estate, managing foundations with billions in public assets
Issuing its own currency in parallel with HUF
quiz.explanation: Under Governor György Matolcsy, Hungary's National Bank (MNB) established foundations that accumulated billions in public assets including art collections and real estate. Critics described this as a way to move public funds outside normal democratic oversight, while the MNB argued it served public interest purposes.

laws.title: Hungary-Serbia Relations and Migration
laws.subtitle: Bilateral Relations and Border Management Agreement
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's border with Serbia became the center of the 2015 European migration crisis. Hungary built a razor-wire fence on the Serbian border (completed October 2015), declared a national state of crisis due to migration, and introduced transit zones where asylum seekers were detained. The ECHR repeatedly ruled against Hungary's pushback practices and detention conditions. Hungary and Serbia coordinate closely on migration deterrence. In 2022, Hungary began pushbacks into Serbia of migrants who had not formally entered through border crossings—a practice documented by human rights organizations.
laws.penalty: Illegal border crossing: criminal prosecution, up to 3 years imprisonment under Hungarian law.
exceptions: Official border crossing points remain open for regular travelers and documented migration
EU citizens have right of free movement through Hungary regardless of border controls

quiz.q: What physical barrier did Hungary construct on its Serbian border during the 2015 migration crisis?
quiz.explanation: Hungary constructed a razor-wire fence along its entire border with Serbia (completed in October 2015) in response to the migration crisis, as approximately 200,000 migrants had crossed into Hungary from Serbia earlier that year. This was followed by a second fence on the Croatian border.

laws.title: Freedom of Assembly and Protest Law
laws.subtitle: Act on the Right to Assembly (2018)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2018 Law on Assembly was criticized for giving police excessive discretion to ban demonstrations and allowing courts to prohibit assemblies as little as 24 hours before they are scheduled. The Constitutional Court partially struck it down (2021) for violating freedom of assembly. However, in practice, pro-government demonstrations have faced no obstacles while opposition protests have been subject to greater scrutiny. The December 2018 'slave law' protests and 2023 teacher salary protests demonstrated that large-scale protests remain possible but face constraints. Public gathering near parliament or the presidential palace requires notification.
laws.penalty: Unlawful assembly: fines. Violent disorder: up to 3 years. Police may disperse without formal authorization in some circumstances.
exceptions: Spontaneous assemblies in response to urgent events have lighter notification requirements
Cultural gatherings and religious processions have different legal framework

quiz.q: What did Hungary's Constitutional Court do to the 2018 Assembly Law in 2021?
options: Partially struck it down for violating freedom of assembly
Ruled it compatible with EU law
quiz.explanation: In 2021, Hungary's Constitutional Court partially struck down the 2018 Assembly Law, finding that certain provisions — including those giving police excessive discretion to ban demonstrations and allowing very short-notice court prohibitions — violated the constitutional right to freedom of assembly.

laws.title: Cultural Heritage and Memory Politics
laws.subtitle: Act on Museums, Public Collections and Libraries (1997, as amended)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's memory politics under Orbán have been highly contested. The House of Terror museum (2002, Terror Háza) focuses primarily on communist-era crimes, with the Nazi Arrow Cross period covered more briefly—critics argue it creates moral equivalence and minimizes Hungary's complicity in the Holocaust. The National Holocaust Memorial Center (Holokauszt Emlékközpont) opened 2004. The 'Great Trianon' national trauma (1920 treaty losing 2/3 of Hungary's territory) is a central political reference for Orbán. The Committee of National Memory controls history curriculum. Statues of Horthy (wartime regent who collaborated with Nazis) have been erected in some towns.
laws.penalty: Holocaust denial: criminal prosecution under criminal code (denial of genocide), up to 3 years.
exceptions: Academic historical debate about degree of complicity is permitted
Religious ceremonies commemorating controversial historical figures are protected

quiz.q: What controversy surrounds Budapest's House of Terror museum?
options: Focuses mainly on communist era, minimizing the Nazi Arrow Cross and Hungary's Holocaust complicity
Refuses to acknowledge the Soviet occupation
Contains inaccurate historical claims about WWII
quiz.explanation: The House of Terror museum (opened 2002) has been criticized for spending most of its space on communist-era crimes while relatively briefly covering the Nazi Arrow Cross period and Hungary's significant role in the Holocaust, raising concerns that it creates false moral equivalence between communist and fascist regimes.

laws.title: Automotive Industry and FDI Law
laws.subtitle: Investment Protection Act and Special Economic Zones
laws.fullDescription: Hungary is a major automotive manufacturing hub—Mercedes-Benz (Kecskemét), Audi (Győr), BMW (Debrecen, opening 2025), Suzuki (Esztergom), and dozens of suppliers. The automotive sector accounts for approximately 30% of Hungarian exports. Battery manufacturing (Samsung SDI, CATL) is the growth sector. Hungary offers generous FDI incentives: individual government investment support (HIPA), free enterprise zones, and subsidized land. The government has used the Law on Strategic Investments to bypass normal planning procedures for large factories. Environmental challenges (water use for battery plants) have sparked local protests.
laws.penalty: Violation of investment contracts: commercial arbitration or national court proceedings.
exceptions: Strategic investments receive expedited government approvals bypassing normal planning
Enterprise zones have special tax and customs treatment

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Hungarian exports does the automotive sector account for?
quiz.explanation: Hungary's automotive manufacturing sector (including Mercedes-Benz, Audi, Suzuki, BMW, and hundreds of component suppliers) accounts for approximately 30% of all Hungarian exports, making it the country's most important industrial sector and a key driver of its export-led economic model.

laws.title: Drug Policy
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code — Narcotics Offenses
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has strict drug laws with no decriminalization or harm-reduction policy shift. Cannabis possession of any amount can lead to prosecution. The new Criminal Code (2012) maintained harsh penalties. Drug offenses represent a significant portion of criminal prosecutions. Hungary rejected EU harm-reduction guidelines. The drug scene in Budapest has grown, particularly around synthetic drugs. Needle exchange programs are limited; drug consumption rooms do not exist. Treatment is primarily abstinence-based. Conservative religious and political values strongly influence drug policy. Precursor chemical regulation targets meth production (a growing problem in some regions).
laws.penalty: Drug possession: up to 2 years (can be avoided with treatment option). Drug trafficking: up to 15 years or life for large quantities or organized crime.
exceptions: Medical cannabis is not approved; CBD products in gray area
Treatment diversion available for first-time personal use offenders

quiz.q: What harm reduction facilities are absent from Hungary's drug policy approach?
options: Drug consumption rooms and comprehensive needle exchange
quiz.explanation: Hungary has rejected drug consumption rooms (safe injection sites) and has very limited needle exchange programs, in contrast to many Western European countries. Hungary's conservative government strongly opposes harm reduction approaches, favoring abstinence-based treatment and criminal enforcement.

laws.title: Internet Freedom and Digital Rights
laws.subtitle: Electronic Communications Act and Digital Rights Policy
laws.fullDescription: Hungary rates poorly on internet freedom (Freedom House: Partly Free). The 2021 amendment to the electronic communications law gave the government power to block websites and services during a 'state of emergency' without judicial oversight. Social media platforms are required to establish Hungarian offices and comply with content removal demands. The government blocked certain LGBTQ+ websites citing the 'child protection' law. GPS tracking, phone tapping, and digital surveillance were used in Pegasus spyware operations. VPN use among journalists and activists has increased. State media dominates the information environment through reach rather than blocking.
laws.penalty: Platform non-compliance with content removal: fines up to 100 million HUF.
exceptions: Academic and research use of otherwise restricted content
News sites with international hosting can continue to operate

quiz.q: What power did Hungary's 2021 amendment to electronic communications law grant the government?
options: Power to block websites during emergency without judicial oversight
Power to nationalize social media platforms
Power to read all electronic communications
quiz.explanation: Hungary's 2021 electronic communications amendment granted the government power to block websites and digital services during a state of emergency without requiring prior judicial authorization, a provision widely criticized as allowing censorship without independent oversight.

laws.title: Agriculture and Land Law
laws.subtitle: Act on Agricultural and Forestry Land (2013)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2013 land law banned foreigners (including EU citizens) from buying agricultural land—a provision ruled incompatible with EU law by the ECJ. Hungary has maintained various restrictions and the Commission continues enforcement proceedings. The National Land Fund manages state agricultural land leased to Hungarian farmers. Generous EU CAP payments flow to Hungarian agriculture—approximately €1.5 billion annually. Large agribusiness interests connected to Fidesz have accumulated significant agricultural land holdings, raising concerns about redistribution. Small family farmers receive support but face competition from politically connected large operations.
laws.penalty: Illegal agricultural land purchase by foreigners: contract nullification, criminal charges for facilitating agents.
exceptions: EU citizens who have been resident farmers in Hungary for 3+ years have some purchase rights
Inheritance of land by EU citizen family members is not prohibited

quiz.q: What did the European Court of Justice rule about Hungary's 2013 agricultural land law?
options: It was incompatible with EU law by banning EU citizens from buying agricultural land
It was fully compliant with EU single market rules
It was acceptable as a national security measure
It was valid under subsidiarity principles
quiz.explanation: The European Court of Justice ruled that Hungary's 2013 agricultural land law was incompatible with EU law because it banned EU citizens from purchasing agricultural land in Hungary, violating the EU's fundamental principle of free movement of capital and the right of EU citizens to invest across member states.

laws.title: Gender Equality and Women's Rights
laws.subtitle: Equal Treatment Authority and Gender Mainstreaming
laws.fullDescription: Hungary formally prohibits gender discrimination under the Equal Treatment Act (2003). However, Hungary was ranked last in the EU Gender Equality Index by EIGE (European Institute for Gender Equality) in 2022. The Fundamental Law defines 'the mother is a woman, the father is a man'—enshrining biological sex in the constitution. Hungary withdrew from ratifying the Istanbul Convention (Council of Europe convention on domestic violence) in 2020, claiming it 'promotes gender ideology.' Women's representation in parliament is low (approximately 13%). Orbán's rhetoric has consistently emphasized women's role as mothers.
laws.penalty: Gender discrimination in employment: Equal Treatment Authority enforcement and court remedies.
exceptions: Positive discrimination programs for women in some sectors are permitted
Religious organizations may apply their ethos in employment of their own staff

quiz.q: What international convention did Hungary refuse to ratify in 2020, claiming it promoted 'gender ideology'?
options: Istanbul Convention on violence against women
Council of Europe's Equal Pay Charter
quiz.explanation: Hungary refused to ratify the Istanbul Convention (the Council of Europe Convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence) in 2020, with the government claiming it promoted 'gender ideology.' Hungary was one of only a few Council of Europe members to refuse ratification.

laws.title: Ombudsman and Oversight Institutions
laws.subtitle: Commissioner for Fundamental Rights Act (2011)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has an Ombudsman (Commissioner for Fundamental Rights, Alapvető Jogok Biztosa) who investigates state abuses. After 2011, the Data Protection Commissioner and the Children's Rights Ombudsman were merged into the Ombudsman's office—some argue this weakened specialized oversight. The State Audit Office (ÁSZ) audits public finances but has been criticized for selective enforcement against opposition-controlled municipalities while avoiding government-connected entities. The Integrity Authority was created in 2022 under EU pressure to combat corruption. Civil society organizations such as Helsinki Committee Hungary have provided oversight where official bodies fall short.
laws.penalty: Government bodies found by Ombudsman to violate rights: recommendations for correction (non-binding but politically significant).
exceptions: Military and intelligence services have limited Ombudsman oversight
President's personal decisions outside formal executive functions

quiz.q: What happened to Hungary's specialized Data Protection Commissioner and Children's Rights Ombudsman in 2011?
options: Merged into the general Ombudsman (Commissioner for Fundamental Rights) office
quiz.explanation: Hungary's 2011 reforms merged the separate Data Protection Commissioner and Children's Rights Ombudsman into the general Office of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights (Ombudsman), a restructuring critics argued weakened specialized oversight in these important areas.

laws.title: Infrastructure and Public Transport
laws.subtitle: National Infrastructure Development Act
laws.fullDescription: Hungary invested heavily in infrastructure through EU cohesion funds. The M0 ring road around Budapest, M4, and other motorways were completed with EU funding. Budapest's BKK public transport is operated by the city—a source of conflict when the opposition controlled Budapest City Hall (2019-2024) and the national government withheld infrastructure funding. The Budapest-Warsaw rail modernization and a controversial Chinese-funded rail line (Budapest-Belgrade) using a non-transparent procurement process raised EU concerns. The government accepted Chinese financing for the railway over EU procurement rules, leading to a specific EU investigation. High-speed rail development is limited.
laws.penalty: Public procurement violations in infrastructure: OLAF investigation, fund recovery, criminal referral.
exceptions: EU-funded projects must follow EU procurement rules
State security infrastructure has different procurement rules

quiz.q: What controversial rail project involving Chinese financing led to EU procurement concerns?
quiz.explanation: The Budapest-Belgrade railway modernization project, financed by Chinese state loans and awarded to a Chinese state construction company, bypassed EU public procurement rules (the government classified it as secret for 10 years). The EU launched an investigation into the procurement process, and Hungary was required to renegotiate some aspects.

laws.title: War Crimes and Historical Accountability
laws.subtitle: Criminal Code — Crimes against Humanity
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has very few convictions for WWII-era crimes. The Arrow Cross regime collaborated in the murder of 500,000+ Hungarian Jews. SS-Obersturmführer László Csatáry was identified as a WWII war criminal in Hungary and died before trial (2013) at age 98. Post-communist Hungary prosecuted some communist-era crimes (the 'salvo' shootings of 1956 revolutionaries). The 1994 statute of limitations reform allowed some prosecution of communist crimes. History curricula and memorial politics remain contested. The ECHR required Hungary to allow the prosecution of Viktor Orbán's father-in-law for communist-era crimes.
laws.penalty: War crimes and crimes against humanity: no statute of limitations. Prosecution remains theoretically possible for surviving perpetrators.
exceptions: Statute of limitations expired for most Nazi-era perpetrators who survived to present day
Some acts from communist era were not classified as crimes at the time

quiz.q: Approximately how many Hungarian Jews were murdered during the Holocaust under Hungary's Arrow Cross collaboration?
quiz.explanation: More than 500,000 Hungarian Jews were murdered during the Holocaust, primarily in 1944 when Hungary's Nazi-collaborating Arrow Cross regime facilitated deportations to Auschwitz-Birkenau with extraordinary speed and thoroughness. This represented approximately 70% of Hungary's pre-war Jewish population.

laws.title: Housing Law and Homelessness Criminalization
laws.subtitle: Act on Misdemeanors (2012) — Rough Sleeping
laws.fullDescription: Hungary amended its Fundamental Law in 2018 to allow the criminalization of homelessness—specifically 'habitual residence in public spaces.' Budapest's rough sleepers could be arrested and fined or imprisoned. The Constitutional Court had previously struck down Budapest's anti-homeless ordinances, prompting the constitutional amendment to avoid judicial review. Amnesty International and the ECHR criticized this as criminalizing poverty. The practical enforcement varied, with some police applying the law strictly and others less so. Social housing provision is limited; eviction protections are weak.
laws.penalty: Habitual residence in public space: misdemeanor, fine, or up to 60 days detention. Repeat offending: possible imprisonment.
exceptions: Emergency shelter capacity is checked before enforcement in extreme weather
Social services referral is supposed to precede prosecution

quiz.q: Why did Hungary amend its Fundamental Law (constitution) in 2018 regarding homelessness?
options: To circumvent Constitutional Court rulings that had struck down anti-homeless ordinances
To provide constitutional right to housing
quiz.explanation: Hungary amended its Fundamental Law in 2018 specifically to allow criminalization of homelessness after the Constitutional Court had struck down Budapest's anti-homeless ordinances as unconstitutional. By embedding the policy in the constitution itself, the government prevented further Constitutional Court review.

laws.title: Competition Law and State Aid
laws.subtitle: Competition Act (1996) and Gazdasági Versenyhivatal
laws.fullDescription: The Hungarian Competition Authority (GVH) enforces competition law based on EU model, prohibiting cartels, abuse of dominance, and unauthorized mergers. Hungary's competition law has generally followed EU standards. However, the GVH has been seen as less active against politically connected entities. State aid rules create tension between Hungary's industrial policy (supporting domestic champions and offering FDI incentives) and EU state aid law. The retail chain nationalization concerns, state intervention in the energy sector, and preferential treatment for connected businesses all raise state aid questions litigated with the European Commission.
laws.penalty: Cartel conduct: up to 10% of annual turnover. Abuse of dominance: significant fines. Criminal referral for hardcore cartels.
exceptions: De minimis aid below €200,000 over 3 years exempt
Block exemptions for R&D, SME, regional, and training aid

quiz.q: What is the name of Hungary's competition enforcement authority?
quiz.explanation: The GVH (Gazdasági Versenyhivatal — Hungarian Competition Authority) is Hungary's independent competition regulator, responsible for enforcing competition law, investigating cartels and abuse of dominance, and reviewing major mergers, broadly following EU competition law standards.

laws.title: 2022 Election and Opposition Challenge
laws.subtitle: Electoral Law and Unified Opposition Campaign
laws.fullDescription: In Hungary's 2022 parliamentary elections, six opposition parties formed an unprecedented unified list behind joint PM candidate Péter Márki-Zay. Despite the unified opposition, Fidesz won 68% of seats with 54% of votes. OSCE observers criticized the election for unequal campaign conditions, state media bias, campaign finance opacity, and gerrymandered constituencies. The election was held as Russia's invasion of Ukraine began—Orbán framed the election as a choice between 'war' (opposition) and 'peace' (Fidesz). The opposition blamed the electoral rules and information environment for the result. Péter Magyar emerged as a new opposition leader in 2024.
laws.penalty: Electoral irregularities: complaints to National Election Commission; final appeal to Kúria (Supreme Court).
exceptions: Campaign activities on election day itself are prohibited
State resources used for government communications are not counted as campaign spending

quiz.q: What strategy did Hungary's opposition parties use in the 2022 election against Fidesz?
options: Formed a unified list with a single joint PM candidate (Péter Márki-Zay)
Boycotted the election to delegitimize it
Filed international legal complaints before voting
Ran independent candidates in all constituencies
quiz.explanation: Six Hungarian opposition parties formed an unprecedented unified list with a single joint prime ministerial candidate (Péter Márki-Zay) for the 2022 election. Despite this strategy, Fidesz won 68% of seats with 54% of votes, demonstrating the extent to which the electoral system favors the ruling party.

laws.title: Roma Integration Policy
laws.subtitle: National Social Inclusion Strategy
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's Roma population (700,000-800,000, about 7-8% of population) faces the most severe socioeconomic disadvantage of any group. Life expectancy is 10-15 years lower than non-Roma Hungarians. School segregation persists despite EU court rulings against it. The NSIS (National Social Inclusion Strategy) provides a policy framework. EU structural funds finance Roma integration programs. Employment rates among Roma are far below the national average. Forced sterilization of Roma women was documented in earlier decades; accountability has been limited. The ECHR has repeatedly found Hungary guilty of discriminatory treatment of Roma.
laws.penalty: School segregation: ECHR rulings against Hungary. Discrimination: Equal Treatment Authority remedies.
exceptions: Positive action in employment and education targeting Roma is permitted under EU law
EU cohesion funds specifically allocated for Roma integration measures

quiz.q: What is the estimated percentage of Hungary's population that is Roma?
quiz.explanation: Hungary's Roma population is estimated at 700,000-800,000 people, representing approximately 7-8% of the total population. They face the most severe socioeconomic disadvantage of any group in Hungary, with the ECHR having repeatedly found Hungary in violation of anti-discrimination standards.

laws.title: Traffic Law and DUI
laws.subtitle: Road Traffic Act (1988, as amended)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has a zero-tolerance blood alcohol limit for driving—0.00% BAC allowed, one of the strictest in Europe. Even one drink can result in criminal proceedings. Random breathalyzer checks are common. The penalty points system was introduced in 2000. Hungary's road fatality rate has improved significantly but remains above EU average. Speed cameras are widespread. 'Közlekedési garancia' (traffic guarantee) points prevent license renewal for serious violations. The transport police (közlekedési rendőrség) enforce traffic law. Drug driving testing was expanded in 2014.
laws.penalty: Any measurable BAC while driving: suspension and fine. Over 0.08%: criminal prosecution, up to 2 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Professional drivers face immediate license suspension for any offense
Emergency vehicle exemptions from some traffic rules when responding

quiz.q: What is Hungary's blood alcohol limit for driving?
quiz.explanation: Hungary has a zero-tolerance blood alcohol limit for drivers — 0.00% BAC is the legal limit. Even one drink resulting in any detectable blood alcohol can result in traffic sanctions. This is one of the strictest drunk driving standards in Europe.

laws.title: Foreign Investment Screening
laws.subtitle: Act on Foreign Direct Investment Screening (2018)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary introduced FDI screening in 2018, requiring government approval for investments in strategic sectors (defense, energy, media, telecommunications, financial infrastructure). The scope was significantly expanded in 2020-2021 covering more sectors. Chinese investments (particularly CATL battery plant, BYD bus factory, and Huawei telecommunications) have proceeded despite Western security concerns. Hungary has been criticized by EU partners for not applying stricter scrutiny to Chinese investments, particularly in telecommunications infrastructure. The screening mechanism is used selectively with politically connected investments often proceeding without friction.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized investment in strategic sectors: forced divestment and fines up to 10% of investment value.
exceptions: Investments from 'friendly nations' (Hungary's assessment) may proceed with simplified screening
Small investments below financial thresholds exempt from screening
laws.sourceLabel: Hungarian Ministry of Technology and Industry

quiz.q: Which Chinese company's Hungarian telecommunications activities have drawn Western security criticism?
quiz.explanation: Huawei's significant role in Hungary's telecommunications infrastructure, including participation in 5G network development, has drawn criticism from EU partners and the US. Unlike many Western countries that have restricted Huawei, Hungary has allowed the company to proceed, reflecting its closer-than-average ties with China.

laws.title: COVID-19 Emergency Response
laws.subtitle: Government Decree Powers During COVID Pandemic
laws.fullDescription: Hungary declared a state of danger in March 2020 and the Orbán government was granted unlimited decree powers by parliament. Hungary was one of Europe's first countries to use Sputnik V (Russian) and Sinopharm (Chinese) vaccines—before EU approval. This created complications for EU health certificates. Hungary's vaccination rate eventually reached EU levels. The unlimited emergency powers (without sunset clause initially) allowed the government to rule by decree across all policy areas, not just health. Civil liberties organizations documented over 100 unrelated policy changes made under COVID emergency powers.
laws.penalty: COVID rule violations: fines by police. Spreading COVID misinformation: up to 5 years imprisonment (broadly drafted law).
exceptions: Religious services were permitted with some restrictions (favored treatment)
Essential businesses could operate under distancing rules

quiz.q: Which vaccines did Hungary use that drew controversy before EU regulatory approval?
quiz.explanation: Hungary was the first EU member state to approve and use both Russia's Sputnik V vaccine and China's Sinopharm vaccine, before they received EU EMA authorization. This caused complications for EU COVID digital certificates since other EU states did not recognize these non-EMA-approved vaccines.

laws.title: Public Media Capture
laws.subtitle: Media Services Act and KESMA Foundation
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's public media (MTVA — Hungarian Television and Radio) was restructured under the 2010 Media Act into a single entity under the Media Council (staffed with Fidesz appointees). The public media operates as a government mouthpiece—broadcasting government messaging 24/7, avoiding critical coverage, and ignoring opposition events. Private pro-government media was consolidated into the KESMA Foundation in 2018 (receiving EU merger block exemption for 'public interest' reasons). KESMA became the largest media group in Hungary with 500+ outlets. State advertising exclusively flows to KESMA and pro-government media, economically strangling independent outlets.
laws.penalty: Independent media outlets violating Media Council rules: fines; public media is exempt from equivalent scrutiny.
exceptions: International media (CNN, BBC, Euronews) freely accessible via cable/satellite
Online independent media (444.hu, Telex) operate outside KESMA structure

quiz.q: What is KESMA in the context of Hungarian media?
options: A pro-government media foundation consolidating 500+ outlets
An online press freedom advocacy organization
quiz.explanation: KESMA (Central European Press and Media Foundation) is a pro-government media foundation that consolidated over 500 Hungarian media outlets in 2018, including newspapers, TV channels, news portals, and radio stations, creating the dominant media conglomerate in Hungary with exclusive access to government advertising revenue.

laws.title: Food Safety and Agriculture Standards
laws.subtitle: Food Chain Safety Act (2008)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's food safety is regulated by the National Food Chain Safety Office (NÉBIH). Hungary has stringent GMO restrictions — GM crops are prohibited under the constitution (Article P). Hungary has lobbied against GM food in EU. Hungarian food products (Tokaj wine, Mangalica pork, Szegedi paprika) have EU Protected Designations. The agricultural sector is a significant employer and political constituency. Food chain safety incidents (contaminated paprika, etc.) are investigated by NÉBIH. Organic farming has grown significantly. Hungary's food exports (€10 billion+ annually) are significant.
laws.penalty: Food safety violations: fines up to 100 million HUF, business closure, criminal prosecution for serious violations.
exceptions: Traditional home food production for personal consumption has simplified rules
Small farmers below production thresholds have lighter compliance requirements

quiz.q: What makes Hungary's constitution unusual regarding genetically modified organisms?
options: It explicitly prohibits GM crops in the country
It requires referendum for any GMO policy change
It bans GMO imports from EU states
quiz.explanation: Hungary's Fundamental Law (constitution) explicitly prohibits genetically modified crops in Hungary — one of very few countries with a constitutional GMO ban. This reflects both environmental concerns and Hungary's positioning of traditional Hungarian food production as a national identity element.

laws.title: Cybersecurity Law
laws.subtitle: Cybersecurity Act (2023) and Digital Infrastructure Protection
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's 2023 Cybersecurity Act (implementing EU NIS2 Directive) establishes comprehensive cybersecurity obligations for operators of essential services and digital service providers. The SZTFH (Supervisory Authority for Regulated Activities) oversees cybersecurity compliance. The Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK) has offensive and defensive cyber capabilities. Hungary has been a target of state-sponsored cyberattacks (reportedly from Russia and others). The government's use of Pegasus spyware demonstrates that Hungary is also a significant cyber attacker domestically. Critical infrastructure protection (energy grids, water systems, financial networks) is mandated.
laws.penalty: Cybersecurity incident non-reporting: fines up to 0.5% of global annual turnover for essential entities. Cyber attacks: up to 8 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Small digital service providers below revenue and user thresholds have simplified requirements
Academic research cybersecurity with prior authorization

quiz.q: What EU directive did Hungary's 2023 Cybersecurity Act implement?
quiz.explanation: Hungary's 2023 Cybersecurity Act implemented the EU's NIS2 Directive (Network and Information Security Directive 2), which significantly expanded cybersecurity obligations across Europe for operators of essential services and digital service providers in sectors like energy, transport, banking, and digital infrastructure.

laws.title: Cultural Policy and National Identity
laws.subtitle: Cultural Strategy and Act on the Protection of Cultural Heritage
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's cultural policy under Orbán heavily emphasizes national identity, Christian heritage, and resistance to 'Western liberal ideology.' The government funds traditional arts generously while progressive or critical arts face defunding. The Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA) was given veto power over state arts funding. Prominent Hungarian artists and intellectuals have faced pressure or left the country. The Hungarian National Museum and National Gallery are major cultural institutions. Budapest has been designated European Capital of Culture multiple times. The state funds Hungarian-language culture in neighboring countries (particularly Romania's Transylvania).
laws.penalty: Cultural heritage damage: up to 3 years imprisonment. Unauthorized export of national heritage items: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Religious cultural objects under church ownership have different preservation rules
Private collections not on national register have lighter protection requirements

quiz.q: What power was given to the Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA) over state cultural funding?
options: Veto power over state arts funding decisions
quiz.explanation: Hungary's government gave the Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA) — a pro-government body — veto power over state arts funding decisions, effectively allowing it to channel funding to government-aligned artists and cultural projects while defunding progressive or critical voices in Hungarian culture.

laws.title: Water Rights and Danube Management
laws.subtitle: Water Management Act (1995, as amended)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary sits in the middle of the Danube Basin—a major water resource. The Tisza River flooding is a recurring challenge. The Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros ICJ case (1997) established Hungary's right to modify its treaty obligations for environmental reasons. Groundwater protection is critical—Hungary has significant thermal spring resources (Budapest's famous bath culture). The EU Water Framework Directive is implemented. Industrial pollution incidents (the 2010 Ajka red mud spill that killed 10 and devastated communities) tested environmental liability law. Climate change is increasing drought risk in eastern Hungary.
laws.penalty: Water pollution causing death: up to 10 years imprisonment. Industrial spill non-reporting: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Agricultural irrigation withdrawals under licensing have seasonal exemptions
Thermal bath operators have specific water use permits

quiz.q: What 2010 environmental disaster in Hungary killed 10 people and contaminated rivers with toxic sludge?
quiz.explanation: The 2010 Ajka red mud disaster occurred when a reservoir containing caustic red mud (toxic waste from alumina production) at the Ajkai Timföldgyár plant burst, releasing approximately 1 million cubic meters of toxic sludge that killed 10 people, injured 150, and contaminated the Danube tributary system.

laws.title: Aviation and Budapest Airport
laws.subtitle: Aviation Act and Airport Privatization Issues
laws.fullDescription: Budapest Liszt Ferenc International Airport (BUD) was privatized to a consortium in 2004 but the Hungarian government announced its repurchase in 2022 for approximately €3 billion—part of the national strategic asset reacquisition policy. The repurchase was financed by Chinese loans (from China Export-Import Bank), raising strategic concerns. Wizz Air (a major European low-cost carrier) is Hungarian-founded and headquartered in Budapest. Hungarian Aviation Authority oversees civil aviation safety. The re-nationalization of the airport was seen as part of a broader pattern of bringing strategic assets under government control.
laws.penalty: Aviation safety violations: license revocation, fines. Unauthorized air operations: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: State military aviation operates under separate Defence Ministry authority
Emergency landing rights cannot be denied regardless of permit status

quiz.q: How did Hungary finance the repurchase of Budapest Liszt Ferenc International Airport in 2022?
options: Chinese loans from China Export-Import Bank
quiz.explanation: Hungary's repurchase of Budapest Airport for approximately €3 billion in 2022 was financed partly through Chinese loans from the China Export-Import Bank—the same lender financing the Budapest-Belgrade railway. This deepened Hungary's financial ties with China, drawing concern from EU partners and the US.

laws.title: Police Powers and Accountability
laws.subtitle: Police Act (1994, as amended 2022)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary's police (Rendőrség) underwent significant expansion of powers in the 2022 amendment. Police can now enter private property, use force, and conduct certain surveillance activities with fewer judicial checks. The Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK) has particularly broad powers. Police accountability is weak—the Independent Police Complaints Board was abolished and complaints are handled within the police hierarchy. The ECHR has repeatedly found Hungary in violation of Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment) in cases involving police brutality against Roma. Gendarmerie (Csendőrség) revival was proposed but not implemented.
laws.penalty: Obstruction of police: up to 2 years. Assaulting officer: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Legal right to remain silent during police questioning
Right to legal counsel from arrest

quiz.q: What happened to Hungary's Independent Police Complaints Board?
options: It was abolished and complaints redirected within the police hierarchy
It was merged with the Ombudsman's office
It was replaced by a parliamentary committee
quiz.explanation: Hungary's Independent Police Complaints Board was abolished, with police misconduct complaints now handled within the police hierarchy itself — a system widely criticized as insufficiently independent. The ECHR has repeatedly found Hungary in violation of Article 3 in cases of police brutality, particularly against Roma individuals.

laws.title: Vocational Education and Dual System
laws.subtitle: Vocational Training Act (2019)
laws.fullDescription: Hungary has promoted its German-style dual vocational education system (apprenticeships combining school and workplace learning). The 2019 Vocational Training Act restructured the system, expanding apprenticeship pathways. Cooperation with major manufacturers (Audi, Mercedes, Samsung SDI) has created employer-specific training. However, the reform also reduced general education content in vocational tracks—raising concerns about social mobility and the right to higher academic education.
